Taking a passport size photo at home

Shoot an acceptable passport style photograph with a phone, including background, lighting and the rules that get photos rejected.

What a studio actually gives you

A photo studio provides three things: a plain evenly lit background, diffuse light with no harsh shadow, and a camera far enough away that your face is not distorted. You can reproduce all three at home. What you cannot reproduce is their willingness to reshoot until it works, so plan on taking twenty pictures.

The background

Find a plain wall in white, off white or very light grey. Stand at least a foot away from it, further if you can. Standing against the wall throws a hard shadow directly behind your head, which is one of the most common reasons a photo is rejected.

A plain bedsheet pinned flat works if you have no clear wall, but iron it first. Creases show up clearly and read as a patterned background.

The light

Face a window during the day. Do not stand with the window behind you, or the camera exposes for the bright background and turns your face into a silhouette. Overcast days are better than bright sun, which creates deep shadows under the eyes and nose.

Avoid overhead ceiling lights on their own. They cast shadows downward across the eye sockets, which is exactly where clarity matters most. Turn them off and use the window.

The camera

Use the rear camera, not the selfie camera. The front lens is wide angle and at arm's length it visibly enlarges your nose and narrows the sides of your face. Automated face matching systems are sensitive to that distortion.

Ask someone to hold the phone about five to six feet away and zoom in slightly, or prop the phone up and use the timer. Distance plus zoom gives a flatter, more accurate rendering of your face.

How to stand and what to wear

Face the camera squarely with your shoulders level. Keep a neutral expression with your mouth closed. Eyes open, looking straight at the lens. No cap and no sunglasses. Prescription glasses are usually acceptable as long as there is no glare and the frames do not cover your eyes.

Wear something that contrasts with the background. A white shirt against a white wall merges into one shape and looks poor once cropped. Darker clothing is safer.

Leave space above your head when you frame the shot. Cropping to a tall ratio later will eat into the top of the frame, and if you started tight your forehead gets cut off.

Sizing it afterwards

A passport photograph is conventionally 35 by 45 mm, which is 413 by 531 pixels at 300 DPI. Exam forms vary widely from that and usually specify their own dimensions, so always follow your notification rather than the passport standard.

Several exams now require the date to be printed on the photograph, or that it was taken within the last few months. Check before you shoot, because it is easier to include a date card in the frame than to add one convincingly afterwards.
